title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Small area estimation for Urban Analytics

Urban researchers often want to use survey data at the scale where urban questions are asked: neighbourhoods, census blocks, transport zones, or other local units. This may involve comparing places, monitoring change over time, identifying local inequalities, or linking survey outcomes to area-level conditions. The problem is that most surveys are not designed to support reliable estimates at all geographic levels and time periods. When responses are broken down by area and year, some cells have only a few respondents and others have none.
This gudie sets out a workflow for choosing spatio-temporal Bayesian small-area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics. It focuses on method choice and shows how these approaches can be implemented in INLA.



Bayesian inference and INLA

Bayesian inference is used to combine survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, neighbouring-area structure, year-to-year structure, and uncertainty from sparse cells in one estimation framework. One advantage is that uncertainty of a modelled estimate is returned as posterior distributions for each estimate, which facilitates interpretation in policy contexts.
For code implementation, the examples are fitted with R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, usually much faster than MCMC for this workflow.



Contents

The practical guide covers the SAE methods most relevant to common Urban Analytics survey and auxiliary datasets, with the choice driven by outcome type, available survey information, auxiliary data, and population structure.


Estimation setup
Start by specifying the estimand: outcome, target population, areas, and time periods. This defines the area-time cells that need estimates and the inputs required for each possible route.
Direct estimation
Compute survey design-based estimates and sampling variances for observed area-time cells. If these estimates are precise enough and have adequate coverage, direct estimation may be sufficient.
Fay–Herriot area-level model
Use this route when direct estimates exist but are too noisy or incomplete, and the available auxiliary data are area-level predictors. The model smooths direct estimates across predictors, neighbouring areas, and time periods.
Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model Use this route when survey microdata are available and the outcome can be modelled at respondent or household level. The fitted unit-level relationship is then aggregated to area-time estimates using area-level summaries of the predictors.
Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP)
Use this route when population counts are available for poststratification cells, such as area by age by sex. The model predicts outcomes for each population cell and weights those predictions back to area-time estimates.




Tutorial data

The worked data are synthetic datasets based on the National Survey for Wales. The maps and estimates are workflow outputs, not empirical findings for specific places in Wales. The synthetic dataset construction and preprocessing steps are described in the estimation setup step.



About the project

The tutorial is part of the TRACK-UK project by the City Modelling Lab.
TRACK-UK develops spatial and statistical methods for analysing mobility patterns at fine geographic scales and assessing their implications for transport decarbonisation in the UK. The project works with academic, policy, and industry partners to produce evidence for transport and energy policy.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
1 The Survey Microdata
The analysis uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on three waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW): 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
The raw survey geography and stratification variable is Local Authority, while the estimation domain here is MSOA. The cleaned survey file therefore assigns each respondent to a synthetic MSOA within their Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. These MSOA assignments are for teaching and workflow development only, so the resulting MSOA estimates should not be interpreted as substantive findings about individual places.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution. The synthetic MSOA assignment supports MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



From here on, the survey period labels are simplified to their end year. For example, the 2020-2021 survey wave is labelled as and referred to as the 2021 wave.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
2 Data Preparation Pipeline



Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs



2.1 Defining The Estimand
The estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It should be defined before preparing the survey indicator or choosing a model, because it determines the outcome coding, denominator, target geography, time period, auxiliary predictors, and poststratification requirements.

Estimate what outcome among which population, across which geography and time period.

In spatio-temporal SAE, this estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination is an area-time cell: one observation we want to estimate. In this worked example, one area-time cell is one MSOA in one survey wave year, or an MSOA-year cell.
In this tutorial, the estimand is:






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle for transport frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025






2.2 Preparing The Survey Indicator
Since we are interested in whether adult respondents cycle frequently as a means of transport, we can code the indicator from AtFrqBke, the active-travel frequency question for cycling.

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
Theory in brief



The unit-level route models respondent outcomes directly. For the area-time target \mu_{jt}, a simple mixed-model form is:

Y_{ijt} = \alpha + x_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t + \epsilon_{ijt},

where x_{ijt} contains unit-level predictors, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect v_t can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. To estimate the target for an area-time cell, the fitted model is evaluated using the corresponding population-level auxiliary summaries \bar{x}_{jt}:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{BHF}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,\bar{x}_{jt}).

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle for transport frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




Unit-level SAE models respondent records directly instead of modelling pre-aggregated direct estimates. For our estimand, the Battese–Harter–Fuller candidate models estimate the binary frequent-cycling indicator from survey records using temporal and spatial random effects, with unit-level age, sex, and car_access added across model specifications.
The fitted model is then used to predict the target MSOA-year estimates using MSOA-level summaries of age, sex, and car access, obtained from ONS UK Census 2021. This avoids relying directly on unstable area-level direct estimates, but introduces new assumptions about how adequately area-level summaries represent the population composition.

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
1 Prepare model and aggregation data
Before preparing the model inputs, we create consistent numeric indices for each area and survey year so that INLA can attach random effects to the correct area and period, as well as a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph .adj as input, similar to what we did in the previous FH model estimation.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

We now prepare the two datasets needed for the unit-level INLA workflow:

model_data contains the sampled respondent records used to fit the model.
aggregation_data contains one row for each area-time cell we want to estimate.


1.1 Respondent model data
The respondent model data has one row per sampled person. For this example we use:

indicator as the binary response, our target;
age as a unit-level predictor;
female as a binary unit-level predictor;
car_access as a unit-level predictor;
time_id as the survey wave year identifier;
area_id as the area identifier;

  mutate(female = as.integer(sex == 2))

model_data <- cycling_indicator |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(indicator, area_id, time_id, age, female, car_access) |>

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit linear mixed models to respondent-level records, then use them to predict area-time means. Because the response variable is binary, the fitted values are interpreted as predicted probabilities.
We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:



Model
Name
Specifications




M1
+TempSpatial
Temporal RW1 plus BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+Demographic
M1 plus respondent age and sex


M3
+CarAccess
M2 plus respondent-level car access




m1_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  age +
  female
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  car_access
)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)

Conceptually, the workflow has two steps: fit the respondent-level model, then evaluate it for each area-time. We fit the candidate models using only the sampled respondent rows. The area-time aggregation rows are used later, after model selection, when posterior draws are evaluated at the MSOA-year predictor summaries.

fit_bhf_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)







Note



When fitting unit-level BHF models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) returns fitted values for the respondent rows used in the likelihood.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit and stores the configuration needed for posterior sampling.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we again use WAIC as a first check, a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA. Lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

model_waic <- imap_dfr(

  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
) |>
  arrange(waic)

bhf_best_model <- model_waic |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(model)

bhf_selected_fit <- bhf_fits[[bhf_best_model]]

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
3 Final estimates and uncertainty
We extract predictions for the target area-time rows, marked in the INLA input as row_type == "aggregation". We then report the posterior mean as the final estimate and use the lower and upper bounds of the 95% credible interval to describe uncertainty.

bhf_selected_fitted_values <- bhf_fits[[bhf_best_model]]$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice(which(model_agg_data$row_type == "aggregation"))

final_bhf_results <- bind_cols(
  aggregation_data |> select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id),
  bhf_selected_fitted_values
) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    bhf_estimate = pmin(pmax(mean, 0), 1),
    bhf_variance = sd^2,
    bhf_lower = pmin(pmax(.data[["0.025quant"]], 0), 1), # clipped to [0,1] since estimate is a share
    bhf_upper = pmin(pmax(.data[["0.975quant"]], 0), 1), # clipped to [0,1] since estimate is a share
    bhf_ci_width = bhf_upper - bhf_lower
  )

The scatterplot below shows that the BHF estimates are in fact much smoother than the direct estimates and closer to the Fay–Herriot estimates, as expected from a model-based approach that borrows strength across area-time cells.


Code
direct_estimates <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "freqbike_estimates_direct.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, n, direct_estimate, variance)

    fh_estimate

  left_join(fh_final_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  left_join(direct_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  relocate(direct_estimate, n, .after = time_id)







However, the BHF and Fay–Herriot estimates for each small area can still differ because the two models use the survey information differently. The BHF model is fitted to unweighted respondent records, while the Fay–Herriot model starts from weighted direct estimates and their sampling variances to model area-year estimates. As a result, unstable direct estimates can affect the Fay–Herriot results, whereas the BHF model may be inaccurate if the complex survey design and weights are ignored. In general, for scenarios where rich survey microdata is present, a unit-level approach is preferred.
That said, although the model is fitted with unit-level predictors, the aggregation step relies on strong assumptions about each area’s population composition. Representing age, sex, and car access with area-level summaries, such as mean age, proportion female, and share of households with car access, can hide important compositional differences. Two areas may have similar summaries but very different age-sex-car structures, meaning the model could produce similar estimates even where cycling behaviour differs across specific combinations of these predictors.
This limitation can be addressed by using a poststratification table that contains population counts for the joint distribution of the relevant predictors. This is the logic of Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP), predict the outcome for each poststratification cell, then aggregate those predictions using the corresponding population counts so the final estimates better reflect the target population composition.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Theory in brief



Let c index poststratification cells within area j and time t. The cells are defined by whichever population variables are available for poststratification. In a unit-level MRP approach, a binary cycling outcome can be modelled at the respondent level as

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ijt}) \\
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{ijt}) &=
\alpha + z_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t .
\end{aligned}

where z_{ijt} is a vector of respondent-level predictors used to define or adjust the poststratification cells, \beta contains their coefficients, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model gives predicted cell means for the binary frequent-cycling indicator in each poststratification cell:

\hat{\pi}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c).

The poststratification step combines those cell predictions with population counts N_{jtc} available or estimated for the same cells. Area-time estimates are then population-weighted averages of the cell predictions. 
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\pi}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle for transport frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




MRP extends the unit-level SAE workflow by combining a respondent-level outcome model with a poststratification table describing the target population. For our estimand, we model the binary frequent-cycling indicator using age_band, sex, car_access, and spatial and temporal random effects. We then produce predicted cell means for the binary frequent-cycling indicator for each age_band × sex × car_access population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
In the poststratification step, our poststratification tables, sourced from ONS UK Census 2021, only observes the 2021 population counts for each age_band-sex-car_access cell for each MSOA,. For the 2023 and 2025 estimands, the model can still estimate different area-time outcomes through the temporal and spatial terms, but the poststratification weights are held fixed, assuming that local demographic and car-access composition does not change across the survey years. In other words, N_{jtc} = N_{jc,2021} for all three waves.

text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Before fitting the model with INLA, as in previous methods, we first create consistent numeric indices for each MSOA and survey year, and a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph for the spatial effect for the modelling datasets.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)


model_data <- model_data |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(indicator, age_band, sex, car_access, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)

poststrat_data <- poststrat_data |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(age_band, sex, car_access, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)

    data = model_data,

    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)

text:
3 Poststratification
At this point, having selected our final model, we use poststratification to convert its cell-level predictions into the target MSOA-year estimates. That means, each age_band x sex x car_access cell prediction is weighted by its population count, then aggregated within each MSOA-year. We can apply this calculation using the posterior mean cell values returned above, which gives a simple point estimate for each cell:


Code

  slice(poststrat_cell_rows) |>
  transmute(cell_mean = mean)

area_year_point_estimates <- cell_point_estimates |>
  group_by(area_id, time_id) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_cell_sum = sum(cell_mean * pop_count),
    population_total = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(mrp_point_estimate = weighted_cell_sum / population_total) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, mrp_point_estimate)

However, the final output for SAE also needs uncertainty estimates. To propagate uncertainty through poststratification, we repeat the same population-weighted aggregation across posterior draws.
The function inla.posterior.sample() gives plausible versions of the fitted model. For each draw, we keep the poststratification rows, convert fitted values from the logit scale to the original 0-1 scale, population-weight them within each MSOA-year, and summarise the resulting posterior distribution.

posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(300, mrp_final_fit)

  plogis(as.numeric(draw$latent[predictor_rows, 1])[poststrat_cell_rows])
})

section: 5 Appendix: Enhance shallow poststratification with contextual predictors
text:
5 Appendix: Enhance shallow poststratification with contextual predictors
Sometimes the population table is available for every target year but only at a shallow cell grain. For example, ONS mid-year population estimates can give MSOA-year counts by age and sex, but not by car access. In that setting we can still use MRP, but the model may only specify two unit-level predictors represented in the poststratification table.
That said, contextual predictors can then be added to help explain between-area (or, between-year) variation. Since these predictors vary by MSOA, not by respondent within an MSOA, this is weaker than having unit-level predictors and matching poststratification cells because they cannot represent how cycling behaviour differs between adults with and without car access inside the same age-sex cell.

In the modelling step, the model specification uses age_band and sex as the poststratification-cell predictors, and adds the contextual area predictors directly as fixed effect terms.

shallow_base_formula <- indicator ~
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE

shallow_context_formula <- update(shallow_base_formula, . ~ . +
  age_band +
  sex +
  population_density +
  car_access_hhshare
)

shallow_context_fit <- inla(
  formula = shallow_context_formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = 1,
  data = shallow_model_data,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
)

title: Direct Estimation
text:
Theory in brief



For an area-time cell (j,t), the target is the population mean or proportion:

\mu_{jt} = \frac{1}{N_{jt}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{jt}} y_{ijt}.

If respondent i has inclusion probability \pi_{ijt} and design weight w_{ijt}=1/\pi_{ijt}, the Horvitz–Thompson ratio direct estimate for area-time cell (j,t) is:

\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} =
\frac{\sum_{i \in S_{jt}} w_{ijt} y_{ijt}}
{\sum_{i \in S_{jt}} w_{ijt}}.

title: Direct Estimation
text:
3 Assess precision and coverage
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because it makes three limitations visible:

Uneven temporal and spatial coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and MSOAs, leaving some area-time cells with much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimates over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves, which may reflect real behavioural change or sampling noise.
Zero within-area variance: For binary indicators, small samples can contain only one response value, producing zero or unrealistically low variances.










In case of unstable or unavailable direct estimates (median n = 4, 3 missing direct estimates) at the target area-time scale as seen above, we turn to model-based SAE methods which borrow strength across areas and years and auxiliary predictors.
There are two approaches:

Area-level SAE models stabilise direct area estimates, and
Unit-level SAE models estimate the individual outcome from survey records and aggregate predictions to target area-years.

The choice between the two should be based on the quality of the direct estimates as modelling input and whether the survey microdata can provide unit-level predictors that can explain the individual variability of the indicator in question.

title: Area-Level SAE Modeling (Fay–Herriot)
text:
Theory in brief



The Fay–Herriot model treats each direct estimate as a noisy observation of the true area-time quantity:

\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} = \mu_{jt} + e_{jt}, \qquad
e_{jt} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{jt}),

where \psi_{jt} is the sampling variance estimated from the survey design. The latent area-time mean is then modelled using predictors and an area random effect:

\mu_{jt} = \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{jt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j + v_t.

Here u_j borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity \mu_{jt}. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect v_t can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. The fitted model gives an area-time estimate by combining the direct estimate with the model prediction:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{FH}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu_{jt} \mid \hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt}, x_{jt}).

Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previous step. The Fay–Herriot model treats each direct estimate for an area-time cell, an MSOA-year cell in this example, as a noisy observation of the underlying frequent-cycling rate, using its sampling variance to control how much confidence the model places in that value.
The model then borrows strength across MSOAs and survey years using spatial and temporal random effects. We then test whether mean adult age, car-access household share, and population density improve fit beyond the temporal-spatial structure.

The missing or zero sampling variances of direct estimates need to be handled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly determined by the model predictions.
Because the outcome is binary (1 for cycling frequently, 0 otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of 0 when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.

  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(variance) ~ max_variance,
      variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ variance
    )
  )

text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct estimation is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M1
+TempSpatial
Temporal and spatial effect


M2
+AvgAge
M1 plus mean adult age


M3
+PopDensCarAccess
M2 plus population density and share of HH with car access



The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.







Temporal model
Description




rw1
First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods.


rw2
Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series.


ar1
Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years.










Spatial model
Description




besag
Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation.


bym2
Updated BYM model with a mixing parameter, phi, which indicates how much residual variation is spatially structured.



With only three survey years, rw1 is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, bym2 is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  scaled_mean_age_adult
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare
)


model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +AvgAge" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +PopDensCarAccess" = m3_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)







Note



When fitting area-level FH models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the final estimates for each area-time row.
scale passes the inverse sampling variance to INLA, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
control.family fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit and stores the configuration needed for posterior sampling.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we use WAIC or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

section: 3 Estimation and aggregation with posterior draws
text:
3 Estimation and aggregation with posterior draws
The selected INLA fit gives posterior draws for the fixed effects and the temporal and spatial random effects. For each draw, we evaluate the fitted model at the MSOA-year aggregation rows, using area-level summaries for age, female share, and car access. The final estimate and uncertainty are summaries of those posterior predictions.

set.seed(100)

bhf_posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = bhf_selected_fit
)

latent_names <- rownames(bhf_posterior_draws[[1]]$latent)
fixed_terms <- rownames(bhf_selected_fit$summary.fixed)

fixed_effect_terms <- tibble(
  term = fixed_terms,
  latent_term = paste0(term, ":1")
)

area_effect_terms <- tibble(
  area_inla_id = area_index$area_inla_id,
  term = paste0("area_inla_id:", area_inla_id)
)

time_effect_terms <- tibble(
  time_inla_id = time_index$time_inla_id,
  term = paste0("time_inla_id:", time_inla_id)
)

stopifnot(all(fixed_effect_terms$latent_term %in% latent_names))
stopifnot(all(area_effect_terms$term %in% latent_names))
stopifnot(all(time_effect_terms$term %in% latent_names))

fixed_draws <- sapply(bhf_posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  values <- as.numeric(draw$latent[fixed_effect_terms$latent_term, 1])
  names(values) <- fixed_effect_terms$term
  values
})

area_draws <- sapply(bhf_posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  values <- as.numeric(draw$latent[area_effect_terms$term, 1])
  names(values) <- area_effect_terms$area_inla_id
  values
})

time_draws <- sapply(bhf_posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  values <- as.numeric(draw$latent[time_effect_terms$term, 1])
  names(values) <- time_effect_terms$time_inla_id
  values
})

bhf_draw_matrix <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = nrow(aggregation_data),
  ncol = length(bhf_posterior_draws)
)

for (draw_id in seq_along(bhf_posterior_draws)) {
  fixed <- fixed_draws[, draw_id]
  prediction <- fixed["(Intercept)"] +
    area_draws[as.character(aggregation_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    time_draws[as.character(aggregation_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  if ("age" %in% names(fixed)) {
    prediction <- prediction + fixed["age"] * aggregation_data$age
  }
  if ("female" %in% names(fixed)) {
    prediction <- prediction + fixed["female"] * aggregation_data$female
  }
  if ("car_access" %in% names(fixed)) {
    prediction <- prediction + fixed["car_access"] * aggregation_data$car_access
  }

  bhf_draw_matrix[, draw_id] <- pmin(pmax(prediction, 0), 1)
}

final_bhf_results <- aggregation_data |>
  select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id) |>
  bind_cols(

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
3 Poststratification with posterior draws
At this point, having selected our final model, we use poststratification to convert its cell-level predictions into the target MSOA-year estimates. That means, each age_band x sex x car_access cell prediction is weighted by its population count, then aggregated within each MSOA-year. We first evaluate posterior draws for every poststratification cell; the cell point estimate is the posterior mean.


Code
set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(300, mrp_final_fit)

latent_names <- rownames(posterior_draws[[1]]$latent)
fixed_terms <- rownames(mrp_final_fit$summary.fixed)

fixed_effect_terms <- tibble(
  term = fixed_terms,
  latent_term = paste0(term, ":1")
)

area_effect_terms <- tibble(
  area_inla_id = area_index$area_inla_id,
  term = paste0("area_inla_id:", area_inla_id)
)

time_effect_terms <- tibble(
  time_inla_id = time_index$time_inla_id,
  term = paste0("time_inla_id:", time_inla_id)
)

stopifnot(all(fixed_effect_terms$latent_term %in% latent_names))
stopifnot(all(area_effect_terms$term %in% latent_names))
stopifnot(all(time_effect_terms$term %in% latent_names))

poststrat_fixed_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ age_band + sex + car_access,
  data = poststrat_data
)[, fixed_terms, drop = FALSE]

fixed_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  values <- as.numeric(draw$latent[fixed_effect_terms$latent_term, 1])
  names(values) <- fixed_effect_terms$term
  values
})

area_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  values <- as.numeric(draw$latent[area_effect_terms$term, 1])
  names(values) <- area_effect_terms$area_inla_id
  values
})

time_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  values <- as.numeric(draw$latent[time_effect_terms$term, 1])
  names(values) <- time_effect_terms$time_inla_id
  values
})

poststrat_draws <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = nrow(poststrat_data),
  ncol = length(posterior_draws)
)

for (draw_id in seq_along(posterior_draws)) {
  linear_predictor <- as.numeric(poststrat_fixed_matrix %*% fixed_draws[, draw_id]) +
    area_draws[as.character(poststrat_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    time_draws[as.character(poststrat_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  poststrat_draws[, draw_id] <- plogis(linear_predictor)
}

cell_mean_predictions <- tibble(cell_mean = rowMeans(poststrat_draws))

cell_point_estimates <- bind_cols(poststrat_data, cell_mean_predictions)

area_year_point_estimates <- cell_point_estimates |>
  group_by(area_id, time_id) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_cell_sum = sum(cell_mean * pop_count),
    population_total = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(mrp_point_estimate = weighted_cell_sum / population_total) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, mrp_point_estimate)

  group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
4 Comparative analysis
Compared to estimates obtained from other modelling approaches, the MRP estimates are very close to the BHF estimates. Agreement with the direct estimates is much weaker as expected, reflecting the instability of sparse MSOA-year survey cells. The Fay–Herriot estimates tend to sit lower than MRP for many cells, suggesting stronger shrinkage toward lower area-year rates.

) |>

  mutate(
    direct_ci_width = 2 * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(pmax(variance, 0))
